title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
blurb: Tell scalars from vectors, calculate speed, velocity and acceleration with the right units, and read position-time and velocity-time graphs.
question: A paramedic unit drives 6 km to a call and 6 km back in 20 minutes, speeding up and slowing down on the way. What were its average speed and average velocity, and when was it accelerating?

teach.body: Formally, a scalar is a quantity with magnitude only, and a vector has magnitude and direction. In plain English: a scalar answers 'how much?', a vector answers 'how much, and which way?'. Distance (total path, say 400 m) is a scalar; displacement (straight-line change in position, say 50 m north) is a vector. Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector. Acceleration, force, momentum and weight are vectors; mass, time, energy and temperature are scalars.

teach.caption: A lap of a track: distance 400 m, displacement 0. The direction is what separates each pair.

teach.h: Three formulas to know by heart
teach.body: Average speed = distance ÷ time. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, a = (v − v₀) ÷ t, in m/s². Acceleration means ANY change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down (negative acceleration when it opposes the motion) or changing direction. For constant acceleration the exam gives the longer equations, such as d = v₀t + ½at², in the stem.

teach.caption: Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6 (72 km/h = 20 m/s). Never mix the two in one calculation.

items: Speed: a bus covers 150 km in 2.5 h. 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h.
Acceleration: a car goes from rest to 24 m/s in 6.0 s. a = 24 ÷ 6.0 = 4.0 m/s².
Distance: same car, d = ½ × 4.0 × 6.0² = ½ × 4.0 × 36 = 72 m. Check: average velocity 12 m/s × 6.0 s = 72 m.
Slowing: a cyclist goes from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 4.0 s. a = (4 − 12) ÷ 4.0 = −2.0 m/s².

teach.body: On a position-time graph the slope is velocity: a straight rising line is constant velocity, a flat line is at rest, a curving line means acceleration. On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement. A flat line on a v-t graph is constant velocity, not 'stopped', unless it sits on zero.

Priya, a radiography applicant, drives 30 km to a clinical site in 0.50 h: average speed 30 ÷ 0.50 = 60 km/h. She drives home by the same road, so her round-trip displacement is zero and her round-trip average velocity is zero, even though her average speed stays 60 km/h. On the curved on-ramp her speedometer holds at 50 km/h, yet she is accelerating, because her direction changes.

teach.text: Speed is not velocity, and distance is not displacement: a round trip has zero displacement and zero average velocity. Constant speed on a curve is still acceleration. The slope of a position-time graph is velocity, not acceleration. In ½at², square t and keep the ½. Convert km/h to m/s before mixing units.

items: Scalars: distance, speed, mass, time, energy. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.
Speed = distance ÷ time; velocity = displacement ÷ time; a = (v − v₀) ÷ t in m/s².
Slowing down gives a negative acceleration; turning at constant speed is also acceleration.
Position-time slope = velocity. Velocity-time slope = acceleration; area under it = displacement.
Divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s.

summary: You can now separate scalars from vectors and calculate speed, velocity and acceleration with correct signs and SI units. You can also read slopes and areas on position-time and velocity-time graphs and convert km/h to m/s.

A.q: Which of these quantities is a scalar?
A.why: Speed has magnitude only, so it is a scalar. Its vector partner is velocity.

whyNot.0: Displacement includes direction, so it is a vector.
whyNot.1: Velocity is speed with a direction: a vector.
whyNot.3: Acceleration has a direction (the direction of the change in velocity): a vector.

A.q: A shuttle bus travels 150 km in 2.5 h. What is its average speed?

whyNot.0: Multiplies distance by time (150 × 2.5) instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: Adds distance and time, which have different units.

A.q: Which definition of acceleration is correct?
options: The rate of change of velocity
The rate of change of position
A.why: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, so it includes speeding up, slowing down and changing direction.

whyNot.1: The rate of change of position is velocity.
whyNot.2: Distance covered each second is speed.
whyNot.3: Acceleration is a rate (per second), and it includes changes in direction, not only speed.

B.q: A car speeds up steadily from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5.0 s. What is its acceleration?

whyNot.0: Uses the final velocity (30 ÷ 5.0) instead of the change in velocity.
whyNot.1: Adds the velocities (40 ÷ 5.0) instead of subtracting.
whyNot.2: Multiplies the change in velocity by the time (20 × 5.0).

B.q: A nurse walks 30 m east down a corridor, then 10 m back west. What are her distance and displacement?
B.why: Distance is the total path: 30 + 10 = 40 m. Displacement is the net change in position: 30 − 10 = 20 m east.

whyNot.0: Swaps the two: the path length is 40 m and the net change is 20 m.
whyNot.2: Uses the path length for displacement; walking back reduces the displacement.
whyNot.3: Uses the net change for distance; distance counts every meter walked.

B.q: On a velocity-time graph, an object's line is flat at 6 m/s for 10 s. What does this show?
options: It is stopped at a fixed position
It speeds up at a steady rate
B.why: On a v-t graph the slope is acceleration. A flat line has zero slope: constant velocity of 6 m/s, so a = 0.

whyNot.0: At rest would be a flat line at 0 m/s, not at 6 m/s.
whyNot.1: Steady acceleration would be a straight line with a slope.
whyNot.3: Slowing down would be a line sloping downward.

C.q: A cart starts from rest and accelerates at 3.0 m/s² for 4.0 s. How far does it travel? (d = v₀t + ½at²)

whyNot.3: 12 m/s is the final speed (3.0 × 4.0), not the distance.

C.q: An ambulance travels at 108 km/h. What is its speed in meters per second? (1 m/s = 3.6 km/h)
C.why: km/h to m/s: divide by 3.6. 108 ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s.

whyNot.1: Divides by 60 as if converting hours to minutes only.

C.q: A velocity-time graph shows a cyclist moving at a constant 8.0 m/s from t = 0 to t = 5.0 s. What displacement does the graph show?
C.why: Displacement = area under the v-t line. Here the area is a rectangle: 8.0 m/s × 5.0 s = 40 m.

whyNot.0: Uses ½ × base × height; that is for a triangle, but this area is a rectangle.
whyNot.1: Divides velocity by time; that is not the area.
whyNot.3: A zero slope means zero acceleration, not zero displacement.

reteach.title: The car's three accelerators
reteach.question: A car has a gas pedal, a brake and a steering wheel. Which of them can make the car accelerate?

blocks.body: Velocity is speed plus direction, so anything that changes either one is an acceleration. The gas pedal raises the speed, the brake lowers it (negative acceleration), and the steering wheel changes the direction. The odometer counts distance (every meter driven); the GPS line from home to here is displacement. The speedometer shows speed; add the compass heading and you have velocity.

blocks.text: 'Constant speed' and 'no acceleration' are not the same thing. Only a constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration.

explain.body: Scalars have size only; vectors add direction. Each motion scalar has a vector partner: distance and displacement, speed and velocity.

test.q: Which pair lists a scalar followed by its vector partner?
test.why: Speed (size only) is the scalar; velocity (speed with direction) is its vector partner.

whyNot.0: The order is reversed: velocity is the vector.
whyNot.2: Reversed: displacement is the vector, distance the scalar.
whyNot.3: Acceleration is a vector, and it is not speed's partner.

explain.body: Average speed uses total distance. Average velocity uses displacement. Return to the start and the displacement, and so the average velocity, is zero.

test.q: A courier drives 12 km to a lab and back by the same road in 0.50 h total. What is his average velocity for the trip?
test.why: He ends where he started, so displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0 ÷ 0.50 h = 0 km/h.

whyNot.0: 48 km/h is his average speed (24 km ÷ 0.50 h), not his velocity.
whyNot.1: 24 km is the total distance, not a velocity.
whyNot.3: Uses the one-way distance and leaves out the time.

explain.body: a = (v − v₀) ÷ t. If the final velocity is smaller than the starting one, the answer is negative: the object is slowing.

test.q: A train slows steadily from 20 m/s to 5.0 m/s in 5.0 s. What is its acceleration?
test.why: a = (5.0 − 20) ÷ 5.0 = −15 ÷ 5.0 = −3.0 m/s². Negative because the train is slowing.

whyNot.0: Right size, wrong sign: the velocity falls, so the acceleration is negative.
whyNot.1: Adds the speeds (25 ÷ 5.0) instead of subtracting.

explain.body: Position-time: slope = velocity. Velocity-time: slope = acceleration, area = displacement.

test.q: On a position-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
test.why: Slope = change in position ÷ change in time = velocity.

whyNot.1: Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph.
whyNot.2: Displacement is read from the graph's vertical values, not its slope.
whyNot.3: Distance is not a slope; it is a length of path.
